title: Mapped Types
summary: **Mapped types** transform one type into another by iterating over its keys with `{ [K in keyof T]: ... }` — letting you build `Partial`, `Readonly`, `Pick`, and custom transforms from scratch instead of hand-writing every variant.

subtopics.title: The basic shape: { [K in keyof T]: T[K] }
subtopics.explanation: A mapped type iterates over the union of keys produced by keyof T, binding each one to K, and produces a property for each. { [K in keyof T]: T[K] } is the identity transform — it reproduces T. Everything else is a variation on this skeleton: change the modifiers, change the value type, or remap the key.
subtopics.example: type Identity<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] };

subtopics.title: Adding modifiers (readonly and ?)
subtopics.explanation: You can attach readonly and/or ? in front of the value to make every property read-only or optional. type Partial<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] } makes all properties optional; type Readonly<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] } makes them immutable. The modifier applies uniformly to every mapped property.
subtopics.example: type Readonly<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] };

subtopics.title: Removing modifiers (-readonly and -?)
subtopics.explanation: The minus prefix strips a modifier that already exists on the source type. -readonly removes immutability and -? makes optional properties required. This is how Required<T> ({ [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] }) and Mutable<T> are built — they reverse what Partial/Readonly add.
subtopics.example: type Mutable<T> = { -readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] };

subtopics.title: Transforming the value type
subtopics.explanation: The right-hand side can be any type expression, not just T[K]. You can wrap each value: { [K in keyof T]: T[K] | null } makes every field nullable; { [K in keyof T]: () => T[K] } turns each value into a getter. This is where mapped types become powerful — uniform value transforms across an entire shape.
subtopics.example: type Nullable<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] | null };

subtopics.title: Key remapping with `as`
subtopics.explanation: TypeScript 4.1+ lets you rewrite keys using an `as` clause: { [K in keyof T as NewKey]: T[K] }. Combined with template literal types you can prefix keys (`get${Capitalize<...>}`) or, by mapping a key to never, filter it out entirely. This turns mapped types into key transformers, not just value transformers.
subtopics.example: type Getters<T> = { [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: () => T[K] };

subtopics.title: Building Partial and Pick from scratch
subtopics.explanation: The standard library utilities are themselves mapped types. Partial<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] }. Pick<T, Keys> = { [K in Keys]: T[K] } where Keys is constrained to keyof T. Understanding these means you can read and write any of the built-ins and create your own when none fit.
subtopics.example: type Pick<T, K extends keyof T> = { [P in K]: T[P] };

subtopics.title: Filtering keys via never
subtopics.explanation: When a key is remapped to never in the `as` clause, that property is omitted from the result. This is the standard idiom for conditionally dropping keys — e.g. removing all function-valued properties — by combining `as` with a conditional type that yields never for unwanted keys.
subtopics.example: type NonFns<T> = { [K in keyof T as T[K] extends Function ? never : K]: T[K] };

foundations.overview: A mapped type is a generic type that produces a new object type by walking over the keys of an existing one and emitting a (possibly transformed) property for each. It is the type-system equivalent of Array.map or a for...in loop, but operating over keys at compile time. With modifiers, value transforms, and key remapping you can express almost any structural transformation declaratively.
foundations.formalDefinition: A mapped type has the form { [K in Keys]: ValueType } where Keys is a union of property keys (usually keyof T), K is bound to each key in turn, and ValueType (often referencing K via T[K]) determines the property type. Optional modifiers readonly/?, their removal forms -readonly/-?, and an `as` key-remapping clause may be applied.
foundations.whyItMatters: Mapped types are how TypeScript's entire utility-type library (Partial, Required, Readonly, Pick, Record) is implemented, and they let you keep many derived types in sync with a single source of truth. Interviewers use them to test whether you can manipulate types programmatically rather than copy-pasting variants.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a mapped type as Array.map for object keys: keyof T is the array of keys, [K in ...] is the loop variable, and the body is what each key produces. Modifiers are like options you toggle on every iteration.
foundations.browserPerspective: Mapped types are entirely compile-time. They are erased during compilation and emit no JavaScript, so they have zero runtime presence in the browser — they only shape what the compiler allows.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Deriving a form-state type where every field is optional during editing, building immutable config types, generating event-handler maps ({ onClick, onHover }) from an event union, and creating DTO variants (a create-input type from an entity by omitting id/timestamps).
foundations.businessImpact: Keeping derived types generated from one source eliminates drift between, say, an entity and its API payloads, reducing the bugs and rework that come from manually-maintained parallel type definitions.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Teams define a domain model once and mechanically derive partial, read-only, and input variants, so a field added to the model propagates everywhere automatically instead of being updated by hand in many places.
foundations.performanceImpact: No runtime cost. Very large or deeply recursive mapped types (especially with key remapping over big unions) can slow type-checking and editor responsiveness, so prefer the simplest mapping that solves the problem.
commonUseCases: Building form/draft state where every field is optional (Partial<T>)
Producing immutable config or frozen state types (Readonly<T>)
Generating getter/handler maps with key remapping (`as`)
Deriving API input DTOs by transforming or filtering an entity's keys

commonMisconceptions.myth: Mapped types can iterate over arbitrary runtime objects.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They operate only on the static type's keys at compile time and are erased before any code runs; they cannot inspect a value at runtime.

commonMisconceptions.myth: readonly and ? can only be added, never removed.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The -readonly and -? prefixes strip modifiers that the source type already has, which is exactly how Required<T> and Mutable<T> work.

steps.name: Compute keyof T
steps.detail: keyof User resolves to the union 'id' | 'name' — the set of keys to iterate over.

steps.name: Bind K to each key
steps.detail: The mapped type loops: first K = 'id', then K = 'name', emitting one property per key.

steps.name: Apply the modifier
steps.detail: The readonly prefix is attached to every emitted property, making each one immutable.

steps.name: Resolve the value type
steps.detail: T[K] indexes the original type: T['id'] is number, T['name'] is string.

steps.name: Assemble the result
steps.detail: The output type is { readonly id: number; readonly name: string } — User with all fields frozen.

codeLab.title: Implement Mutable<T> from scratch
codeLab.instructions: Write a mapped type Mutable<T> that strips readonly from every property of T using the -readonly modifier. Reassigning a field on a Mutable<Config> should be allowed.
hints: Use the mapped-type skeleton { [K in keyof T]: T[K] }.
Prefix the index signature with -readonly to remove immutability.

debuggingLab.title: Modifier in the wrong place
debuggingLab.symptom: An attempt to make every field optional instead loses the value types or fails to compile because the ? is placed on the value, not the key.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Unioning | undefined onto the value type does not make the property optional — the key must still appear in the object. The optional modifier belongs on the index signature (after the bracket), as [K in keyof T]?, which is what actually lets the key be omitted.
commonMistakes: Confusing 'value may be undefined' with 'property is optional'.
Putting the ? modifier on the right-hand value type instead of after the [K in ...] bracket.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Rewrite the type so every property is genuinely optional (can be omitted), matching Partial<User>.

theory.question: What is a mapped type and how does it work?
theory.directAnswer: A mapped type creates a new object type by iterating over a union of keys — usually keyof T — and emitting a property for each, optionally transforming the modifiers, the value, or the key. It uses the form { [K in keyof T]: T[K] }, which is the type-level analogue of mapping over an object's keys, and it powers utilities like Partial, Readonly, and Pick.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A generic type that produces a new type by binding K to each key in a key union and emitting one property per key.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To derive related types from a single source mechanically instead of hand-writing every variant, keeping them in sync.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: keyof T yields a union of keys; [K in ...] iterates that union; the value expression (often T[K]) types each property; modifiers and an `as` clause can transform keys/values. It is fully evaluated by the compiler and erased at emit.

theory.whyImportant: Mapped types are the foundation of TypeScript's utility-type library and a strong signal of advanced type fluency in interviews.
theory.realWorldExample: Partial<FormValues> lets a form hold a draft where any field may be missing while editing, derived automatically from the full value type.

nestedTopics.title: keyof + in
nestedTopics.explanation: keyof T gives the key union; [K in ...] iterates it, binding K to each key.

nestedTopics.title: Modifiers
nestedTopics.explanation: readonly and ? can be added; -readonly and -? remove them from the source.

nestedTopics.title: Key remapping
nestedTopics.explanation: The `as` clause rewrites or filters keys (mapping to never drops them).

followUps.question: How do you make every property optional?
followUps.answer: Put the ? modifier after the index signature: { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] }, which is exactly Partial<T>.

followUps.question: Do mapped types exist at runtime?
followUps.answer: No — they are erased during compilation and emit no JavaScript, so they only constrain the compiler.

theory.question: What do the -readonly and -? modifiers do, and when would you use them?
theory.directAnswer: The minus-prefixed modifiers remove a modifier the source type already has: -readonly strips immutability so properties become writable, and -? makes optional properties required. They are used to build the inverses of Readonly and Partial — namely Mutable<T> = { -readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] } and Required<T> = { [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] }.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Modifier-removal operators applied inside a mapped type's index signature.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Because by default a mapped type preserves the source's modifiers; you need an explicit way to subtract them.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Prefixing the modifier with - subtracts it during the mapping, regardless of whether each individual property had it, producing a uniformly writable or required result.

theory.whyImportant: Knowing both directions shows you understand that modifiers are independently addable and removable — a common advanced-TS interview probe.
theory.realWorldExample: Required<Options> is handy after merging user-supplied partial options with defaults: the result has every field present, so downstream code never re-checks for undefined.

nestedTopics.title: Modifier preservation
nestedTopics.explanation: Without a +/- prefix, the source's existing readonly/? are carried through unchanged.

nestedTopics.title: Required<T>
nestedTopics.explanation: Implemented as { [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] }.

followUps.question: Does -? also remove | undefined from the value?
followUps.answer: Yes — Required<T> with -? strips the optional modifier and the implicit undefined it adds, leaving the bare value type.

scenario.question: Your codebase manually maintains a CreateUserInput type alongside the User entity, and they keep drifting apart whenever someone adds a field. How would you use mapped types to fix this?
scenario.directAnswer: Derive the input type from the entity instead of duplicating it. Use a mapped type (composed with Omit) like type CreateUserInput = Omit<User, 'id' | 'createdAt'>, or write a custom mapped type that drops server-generated keys via key remapping to never. Now adding a field to User automatically appears in CreateUserInput, eliminating drift.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Replacing a hand-written parallel type with one mechanically derived from the source via mapped/utility types.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Manually maintained parallel types inevitably drift; deriving them keeps a single source of truth.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Omit (a mapped type using key remapping with `as ... never`) iterates the entity's keys, dropping the excluded ones, so the input type tracks the entity automatically.

scenario.whyImportant: Real apps have many shape variants per entity; deriving them is the difference between maintainable and bug-prone type code.

nestedTopics.title: Omit via key remapping
nestedTopics.explanation: Omit<T, K> maps keys, sending excluded keys to never so they vanish.

nestedTopics.title: Single source of truth
nestedTopics.explanation: Derived types update automatically when the source entity changes.

followUps.question: What if some fields should be required on input but optional on the entity?
followUps.answer: Compose mapped types: start from Omit, then apply Required to the subset of keys that must be present, e.g. Required<Pick<...>> intersected with the rest.

coding.question: Implement a mapped type Stringify<T> that keeps every key of T but changes each value type to string, and verify it on a sample object.
coding.thoughtProcess: I keep the mapped-type skeleton { [K in keyof T]: ... } so all keys are preserved, but I replace the value expression T[K] with the literal type string. There are no modifier changes, so I just emit string for every property. At runtime I can String() each value to satisfy the produced type.
coding.lineByLine: type Stringify<T> = { [K in keyof T]: string } keeps every key (via [K in keyof T]) but fixes each value type to string. The runtime stringify mirrors this by iterating Object.keys and coercing each value with String(). The result is typed so result.id is string even though the input id was a number.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) over the object's own keys at runtime.

alternativeApproaches.title: Conditional per-key transform
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Combine with a conditional type to stringify only certain value types and leave others intact.
alternativeApproaches.code: type Stringify<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] extends number ? string : T[K] };

followUps.question: How would you preserve readonly/optional modifiers from T?
followUps.answer: Leave the mapped type without +/- prefixes — by default { [K in keyof T]: string } carries the source's readonly and ? modifiers through unchanged.

systemDesign.question: Design a type-safe configuration layer where the same shape must appear as fully-required runtime config, a partial user-override, and a frozen snapshot. How do mapped types let you maintain one source of truth?
systemDesign.directAnswer: Define a single canonical Config interface as the source of truth, then mechanically derive every variant with mapped types: UserOverrides = Partial<Config> for the optional inputs, ResolvedConfig = Required<Config> after defaults are merged, and FrozenConfig = Readonly<Required<Config>> for the immutable snapshot handed to the app. A merge function takes Config defaults plus Partial<Config> overrides and returns Required<Config>, so every layer stays in lockstep with the canonical shape and adding a field updates all variants automatically.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An architecture where one base type generates all derived config shapes via mapped/utility types rather than parallel hand-written definitions.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Config flows through distinct phases (override, resolve, freeze) with different modifier requirements; deriving them prevents drift across layers.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Partial loosens for inputs, Required tightens after defaulting, Readonly freezes for distribution; each is a mapped type over the same Config, so the compiler enforces consistency end to end.

systemDesign.whyImportant: Configuration is a classic place where multiple type variants of one shape coexist; getting it wrong causes undefined-field bugs at runtime, and interviewers probe whether you can structure it cleanly.

nestedTopics.title: Phase-specific variants
nestedTopics.explanation: Partial for inputs, Required post-merge, Readonly for the distributed snapshot.

nestedTopics.title: Single source of truth
nestedTopics.explanation: Every variant is derived from one Config, so changes propagate automatically.

nestedTopics.title: Compile-time enforcement
nestedTopics.explanation: tsc rejects code that treats a Partial as Required, catching missing-default bugs early.

followUps.question: How would you make only a subset of keys overridable?
followUps.answer: Compose Pick with Partial: type UserOverrides = Partial<Pick<Config, 'theme' | 'locale'>> so only the chosen keys are loosened while the rest remain fixed.

followUps.question: How do you guarantee the frozen snapshot is truly immutable at runtime, not just in types?
followUps.answer: Pair Readonly<T> (compile-time) with Object.freeze (runtime), since mapped types are erased and cannot enforce immutability when code runs.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Mapped types form the derivation layer of a typed domain model: a canonical entity type plus mechanically-derived variants (Partial for drafts, Omit-based input DTOs, Readonly snapshots). Centralizing these as named utility types keeps the whole codebase deriving from one source rather than maintaining parallel shapes.
productionDeepDive.performance: Zero runtime cost — mapped types are erased. The cost is compile-time: key remapping over large unions, nested mapped types, and recursion can noticeably slow tsc and the editor's language service, so keep mappings shallow and cache complex derived types behind named aliases.
productionDeepDive.security: Mapped types describe shape, not runtime trust. A Readonly type does not prevent mutation at runtime and a derived input type does not validate untrusted payloads, so pair them with Object.freeze and a runtime validator (e.g. Zod) at trust boundaries.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Encode each transformation once (DraftOf<T>, InputOf<T>, FrozenOf<T>) and reuse it across entities; as the model grows, new fields flow into all variants automatically, keeping type maintenance sublinear in the number of shapes.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Prefer the standard utilities (Partial, Readonly, Pick, Omit, Record) when they fit, and reach for custom mapped types only for transforms they cannot express. Name custom mapped types after intent and document any key-remapping logic, since `as` clauses are easy to misread.
productionDeepDive.observability: Type-level mistakes surface in the editor and in CI via tsc --noEmit. For tricky mapped types, hover-inspect the resolved type or use type-level test assertions (Expect/Equal helpers) to lock in the expected output and catch regressions.

caseStudies.problem: Developers constantly needed optional, read-only, and subset variants of object types.
caseStudies.solution: Shipped Partial, Required, Readonly, Pick, and Record — all implemented as mapped types — as built-ins.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Powerful and reusable, but heavy custom mapped types can slow type-checking and confuse readers.
caseStudies.lessons: Most real-world type derivation can be expressed by composing a few mapped-type-based utilities rather than writing bespoke ones.

keyTakeaways: A mapped type is { [K in keyof T]: ... } — the type-level equivalent of mapping over an object's keys.
Modifiers readonly and ? can be added; -readonly and -? remove them, which is how Mutable and Required are built.
The value expression can transform each property (nullable, getters, stringified), not just copy T[K].
Key remapping with `as` rewrites or filters keys, and mapping a key to never drops it.
Partial, Readonly, Pick, Omit, and Record are all mapped types — learn the skeleton and you can build any of them.
